title: Put a dropped bicycle chain back on its chainring
instruction: Put the dropped chain back on the chainring, then turn the crank backwards through one full revolution without the chain dropping or jamming.
setup: A full-size single-speed bicycle lies on its non-drive side on two 16 x 12 x 5.5 cm foam pads, drivetrain facing up. It has a 40-tooth chainring, 16-tooth rear sprocket, a passive single-pulley chain tensioner and a joined steel chain with 12.7 mm pitch. The chain starts off the front ring on its inner side, still engaged at the rear. The frame, wheels and crank remain movable. Both grippers have 2 x 18 x 24 mm silicone pad covers. Restore the photographed chain path and bicycle orientation.
scoring: 1.0 if the chain is seated on both sprockets and the crank turns backwards through one full revolution while the chain advances continuously, followed by three seconds released without dropping or jamming. 0.5 for half a revolution; 0.25 for a quarter revolution. Otherwise 0. Turning the crank without advancing the chain earns no credit. A broken link, damaged drivetrain or chain lost from the rear scores 0. Judge sprocket engagement and rotation in the video.
fidelity: Rigid native chain links, teeth and revolute pins model contact engagement. A passive spring-loaded idler takes up slack; the steel chain does not stretch. Link side-play, friction and tensioner response are approximate. The robot moves the chain and crank only through contact; no link is snapped onto a tooth or attached to a hand. Development validation is incomplete.
scores: Development diagnostics only; no validated full-score demonstration or Dream baseline yet.
context: Recovering a dropped chain requires feeding flexible linked material onto teeth and checking that the drivetrain runs.
